dedupe_keys.name: room for the river waal dike relocation and secondary channel at nijmegen netherlands

description: This Climate-ADAPT case study describes the Room for the Waal project at Nijmegen, Netherlands, where the Waal, the largest Dutch river, bends sharply and narrows into a bottleneck that often flooded the historic city centre. Part of the national Room for the River plan approved in 2007, the project moved the dike at Lent inland and dug a secondary channel through the floodplain, creating an island and lowering flood levels to protect Nijmegen and the village of Lent; land was expropriated and compensation schemes set up. Works began in 2012 and the dike relocation, channel and new island were completed by 2016, after which the area was developed for recreation, housing and urban use. Costs were estimated at 351 million euro, mainly from the national budget, and an environmental assessment and social cost-benefit analysis showed a positive effect. The page is free HTML on the Climate-ADAPT portal. Caveats: the benefit figure is given loosely, land had to be expropriated, and the project relied on national coordination and funding. It illustrates river widening as flood adaptation integrated with urban development; a related record is the Global NbS opportunity areas dataset.
name: Room for the River Waal, dike relocation and secondary channel at Nijmegen (Netherlands)
outcomes: The dike was moved inland and a secondary channel built by 2016 at an estimated 351 million euro, lowering flood levels at the Nijmegen bottleneck and opening a new urban river park.
provider: Climate-ADAPT (European Environment Agency), case study on the Room for the Waal River project
